tldr: The authors propose PARTS, a framework that concentrates real-world reinforcement learning (RL) on only the specific subtasks where a pretrained robot policy (VLA) tends to fail, drastically boosting long-horizon task success in short training times using residual corrections and local rewards.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of PARTS. On the left, coding agents generate selector, verifier, and reset programs for human-identified bottlenecks. On the right, residual action policies are trained on top of a frozen base model via local RL and success-reweighted retraining.
overview:
Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models handle diverse manipulation skills. However, on long-horizon tasks, they often hit a wall: they repeatedly fail on a few critical, high-precision subtasks—such as inserting an earbud into a tight slot or grasping a tiny part—keeping overall success low.

Collecting additional full-task demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) forces human operators to re-demonstrate easy steps the policy can already perform well, requiring substantial effort. On the other hand, applying real-world RL across the entire task suffers from sparse rewards given only at completion. When the robot fails midway, it receives no learning signal at all, wasting valuable physical rollout budget.

To address this, the authors introduce PARTS (Policy Adaptation with RL on Targeted Subtasks). PARTS freezes the pretrained foundation policy and concentrates RL strictly on the bottleneck subtasks where failures cluster. Once a human defines where failures occur, LLM coding agents generate executable code for when to activate corrections and whether the subtask succeeded. This enables local trial-and-error and automated verification without human interventions during rollouts.

Evaluated on bimanual YAM and single-arm Franka real-robot setups, PARTS improved complete-task success from 32% to 61% and from 50% to 95%, respectively, with only tens of minutes of practice. Compared with conventional methods that fine-tune across the entire task, PARTS achieves significantly higher success rates under the same robot-rollout budget.
contributions: Formulating policy adaptation as local reinforcement learning focused strictly on bottleneck subtasks, rather than re-solving the entire long-horizon task from scratch.
Using coding agents to build policy selectors, success verifiers, and auto-reset programs, eliminating human teleoperation interventions and manual success labeling during RL data collection.
Introducing success-reweighted retraining to leverage rare successes in local trials and prevent exploratory stagnation.
Demonstrating practical effectiveness on bimanual YAM and single-arm Franka platforms, improving full-task success by more than 25% with only tens of minutes of real-world rollouts on average.

sections.heading: The Long-Horizon Barrier: Stop Re-Teaching What Robots Already Do Well
sections.summary: Pretrained VLAs succeed on many steps but fail on specific subtasks requiring millimeter precision. This work keeps what already works intact and repairs only the bottleneck subtasks using residual RL.
sections.details:
Recent VLA models and world-action models (WAMs) provide capable policies by leveraging large robot datasets and visual semantic reasoning. However, full completion rates on long-horizon tasks remain low due to subtle contact dynamics, grasp pose misalignments, and state drift across step transitions.

Most of these failures cluster at specific bottleneck subtasks rather than being spread across the entire execution. In an earbud-casing task, for instance, the robot can easily pick up the earbud, but a slight tilt in the grasp makes inserting it into the hole nearly impossible. Collecting additional full-task supervised demonstrations forces human operators to repeatedly demonstrate the simple behaviors that already succeed, incurring significant manual effort.

Meanwhile, updating policies with real-world RL under sparse, full-task completion rewards yields no learning signal when a rollout fails partway through. Worse, stumbling early in the sequence prevents the robot from ever reaching and practicing the downstream bottlenecks.

To solve this, the authors propose PARTS. It freezes a state-of-the-art pretrained foundation policy, $\pi_{0.5}$, as the base policy and introduces lightweight residual policies only during bottleneck subtasks. Executable programs generated by coding agents automatically handle activation timing and success verification. As a result, the physical robot can practice autonomously without human teleoperation or manual reward labeling.

sections.heading: Beyond Prior Work: From Global Improvement to Failure-Localized Policy Repair
sections.summary: Most real-world RL for long-horizon tasks either attempts global policy optimization across the whole task or relies heavily on human supervision. PARTS innovates with failure-localized policy repair, drastically reducing human oversight via executable code contracts.
sections.details:
### Real-World Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Tasks
Unlike Sim-to-Real transfer, updating policies directly on real hardware always faces data collection costs, reset overhead, and the dangers of unconstrained exploration. Prior work improved sample efficiency by combining demonstrations, residual control, and learned reward functions.

With recent advances in VLA models, methods that fine-tune pretrained models via online RL have emerged, but they tend to improve the entire task globally. In contrast, PARTS adopts failure-localized policy repair. It leaves reliable behaviors untouched and focuses physical rollouts strictly on the few bottlenecks that rate-limit long-horizon task success.

### Reducing Human Supervision in Real-World Adaptation
To ensure safe exploration and prevent failures on physical hardware, human intervention—such as corrective teleoperation, policy switching, and manual success labeling—has been widely adopted. However, requiring constant human oversight does not scale.

Recent methods like UniIntervene (which invokes recovery when value estimates drop) and Robot Trains Robot (which automates protection and failure detection) have been introduced, but they also operate across the full task. Because PARTS restricts practice to bottleneck subtasks, the scope of verification and resetting becomes localized and simple. Automated verifiers and reset programs generated by coding agents can reliably run the learning loop autonomously.

sections.heading: How PARTS Works: Coordinating Frozen Models, Residual RL, and Agent-Generated Code
sections.summary: Keeping the pretrained model frozen, PARTS trains residual policies with TD3+BC to correct targeted degrees of freedom only during bottlenecks. Agent-generated programs handle activation, verification, and resetting, while success-reweighted retraining drives efficient learning from scarce successes.
sections.details:
### Problem Formulation
A pretrained VLA policy (here, $\pi_{0.5}$) outputs action chunks $\bar{A}_t$ (future action sequences) from multi-view images and proprioception. The target task consists of a sequence of $N$ subtasks $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_N$, and a full-task reward $R \in \{0,1\}$ is awarded only when all steps succeed. Because the overall success probability roughly equals the product of subtask success rates $\prod_i p_i$, a few low-performing bottleneck subtasks bottleneck the entire pipeline. PARTS concentrates practice resources on this bottleneck set $\mathcal{K}$.

### Residual RL with TD3+BC
The frozen base model continuously supplies nominal action chunks $\bar{A}_t$. Within bottleneck $k$, a lightweight residual actor $f_{\theta_k}$ outputs normalized corrections $U_{k,t}$. The command sent to the robot is composed as:
$$a_t = \mathcal{C}(\bar{a}_t + M_k \odot B_k \odot u_{k,t})$$
Here, $M_k$ is a binary mask restricting corrections to specific coordinates (such as gripper open/close or translation), and $B_k$ represents physical correction bounds. Irrelevant action dimensions retain the base model output directly, ensuring safe and efficient exploration.

Training uses TD3+BC adapted for action chunks with imitation regularization. The actor maximizes the Critic's Q-value while cloning (BC) residuals from successful trials and regularizing residuals toward zero on failed trials. Reference dropout is also introduced, zeroing nominal inputs with a certain probability to prevent the residual policy from merely copying the base chunks.

### Agentic Scaffolding
Once a human observes a few failures and writes a contract (start conditions, correction axes, success criteria, and action budgets), coding agents (such as Claude Fable 5 or GPT-6 Astra) generate three executable programs:
- **Policy Selector**: Determines when to activate the residual policy based on sensor feedback and geometric predicates.
- **Success Verifier**: Evaluates whether conditions are met at subtask termination and returns a local reward $r_k \in \{0,1\}$. It leverages SAM3 object segmentation and asynchronous queries to a VLM (Gemini-3.7-flash).
- **Auto-Reset Policy**: Determines whether an immediate local retry is feasible on failure, and returns the robot to the initial state upon success (such as placing a grasped part back on the table).

### Success-Reweighted Retraining and Redeployment
Because initial bottleneck success rates are low, successful transitions in the buffer are extremely scarce. Moreover, repeated local resets risk overfitting to specific configurations, leaving the policy unable to handle varied states drifting in from upstream steps. PARTS periodically builds a curated dataset $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_k$ containing all successful trials and a fraction $\rho$ of failed trials, retrains a fresh network, and redeploys it on the robot. This anchors rare success patterns and helps the policy escape local optima.

sections.heading: Real-World Experiments: Millimeter-Level Bimanual Skills Dramatically Improved in Minutes
sections.summary: PARTS was evaluated across three tasks on bimanual YAM and single-arm Franka setups. Under identical robot-rollout budgets, it outperformed full-task RL baselines by more than 25% and confirmed the importance of success-reweighted retraining.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Tasks
Three long-horizon manipulation tasks were evaluated on two physical robot platforms (Figure F3):
1. **Earbud Casing (Bimanual YAM)**: A high-precision task requiring the robot to open the case, hold it with the left arm, insert two earbuds into millimeter-clearance slots using the right arm, and close the lid. Bottlenecks are case preparation (RL0), first insertion (RL1), and second insertion (RL2).
2. **Lego Sorting (Bimanual YAM)**: Sorting 10 Lego bricks into color-coded bins within 150 seconds. Grasping is difficult because the physical bricks are smaller than those in pretraining data, requiring the grasp subtask (RL) to be repeated 10 times.
3. **Cable Routing (Single-Arm Franka FR3)**: Unplugging an Ethernet cable from one router, aligning it, and inserting it into a port on another router. Bottlenecks are alignment and insertion (RL).

### Baseline Comparisons
PARTS was compared against the SFT base policy, DSRL (exploring in latent noise space), EXPO-FT (fine-tuning the full foundation model), and RLT (handing off to RL only during critical phases). For fairness, physical robot rollout time was matched across all methods.

- **Overall Improvements (Q1)**: On cable routing, success doubled from 50% to 95% with just 29 minutes of rollout. On the challenging earbud casing task, complete-task success quadrupled from 32% to 61%, with individual insertion stages gaining 20 to 35 percentage points. Lego sorting progress surged from 54% to 82% in 17 minutes of practice.
- **Comparison to Prior Methods (Q2)**: PARTS consistently outperformed all baselines under the same rollout budgets. Prior approaches re-execute the entire task, wasting time on steps that already succeed and struggling to learn from sparse terminal rewards. Notably, EXPO-FT degraded existing capabilities while updating the foundation backbone, breaking the cable unplugging skill that originally worked.
- **Effect of Retraining (Q3)**: An ablation omitting success-reweighted retraining on the earbud task (hatched bars in the figure) led to overfitting on localized configurations, causing a significant drop in both subtask and full-task success.

captions.F3: Figure F3: The three physical robot tasks used for evaluation. Colored borders in each row indicate active intervention by residual policies specialized for corresponding subtasks: bimanual earbud casing (top), out-of-distribution Lego sorting (middle), and single-arm cable routing (bottom).

sections.heading: Conclusion and Outlook: A New Baseline for Autonomous Policy Improvement
sections.summary: PARTS demonstrates the power of preserving pretrained capabilities while repairing only failing subtasks with minimal human intervention. Future work aims for complete autonomy by automating bottleneck discovery and recovery behaviors.
sections.details:
PARTS shifts the paradigm of fine-tuning pretrained robot policies on long-horizon tasks from full-task re-demonstration to targeted bottleneck practice. By achieving dramatic success gains in tens of minutes of real-world rollouts without continuous human teleoperation or manual reward labeling, it marks a significant step toward practical real-world reinforcement learning.

For future work, the authors highlight three directions: automating bottleneck identification via agents, generating denser subtask reward signals automatically, and learning autonomous recovery phases from failure states. Achieving these capabilities would further minimize human dependence, including physical manual resets.

takeaways: Failures in long-horizon tasks cluster at specific subtasks; freezing the base policy and applying residual RL only to bottlenecks is far more efficient than full-task retraining.
Using coding agents to generate selector, verifier, and reset logic drastically cuts human intervention during RL data collection.
Success-reweighted retraining from replay buffers is crucial to prevent policy overfitting and state distribution collapse during local practice.
Directly updating foundation model weights using sparse task rewards risks catastrophic forgetting, destroying behaviors the robot could already execute.
limitations: Initial bottleneck identification and rough contract definitions (operating bounds and success criteria) still require human observation and setup.
Physical manual resets by humans remain necessary when parts fall off the workspace or when the robot cannot reach objects to reset them autonomously.
VLM-based success verifiers can still misclassify subtle visual distinctions, such as whether an earbud is resting on top of the slot or fully seated inside.
